(Rabbana) — with the implied "they say"; az-Zamakhshari estimated it as: they cry out for help with their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen﴾ what we used to deny; ﴿and we have heard﴾ what we used to reject; and we have seen the truth of Your promise and Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers; and we were blind and deaf, but now we have seen and heard, so send us back to the world.

"Indeed we are certain" (inna muqinun): that is, of the resurrection. This was said by al-Naqqash. It was also said: "We are those who affirm the truth of what the Messenger ﷺ said," as related from Yahya ibn Salam.

"Muqinun" implies a state of having become certain at this moment, that is, when they see and hear. It was also said: the doubts have now been removed from us; we did not reflect in the world, and we were like those who neither see nor hear. It was also said: "To You belongs the proof, our Lord; we have now seen Your messengers and wonders in the world, and heard their speech, so we have no proof left for ourselves." This is a confession from them.

(p-196) This surah is Meccan. It was said that five verses are an exception: from ﴿They forsake their beds﴾ [al-Sajdah 16] to "you used to deny" (tukadhdhibun). Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said that three verses were revealed at Medina: ﴿Is one who was a believer﴾ [al-Sajdah 18]. The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Allah did not send Muhammad to us, and what he brought is only his own fabrication." So this was revealed. Since, before this, He (exalted is He) mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God) from the beginning of creation, which is the first principle, and then mentioned the resurrection and the gathering, which is the second principle, and closed the surah with it, He mentioned at the beginning of this surah the third principle, which is the clarification of the message (risalah).

"Al-Kitab" means the Qur'an. Al-Hufi said: "Tanzil" is a subject (mubtada'), and "la rayba" is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for "tanzil" to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this recited text is a revelation (tanzil), or these letters are a revelation, and "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a substitution (badal) for the letters. Abu al-Baqa' said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a subject, and "tanzil" is its predicate in the sense of "mazil" (a sent-down thing); "la rayba fihi" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "al-Kitab," and the governing element in it is "tanzil"; and "min rabbi al-'alamin" is also connected to "tanzil." It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "fihi," and the governing element in it is the adverbial phrase. It is also permissible for "tanzil" to be a subject, with "la rayba fihi" as the predicate, and "min rabbi al-'alamin" a circumstantial clause, as previously mentioned. It is not permissible on this view for it to be connected to "tanzil," because the verbal noun has already been given as a predicate. It is also permissible for the predicate to be "min rabbi al-'alamin," with "la rayba" a circumstantial clause from "al-Kitab," and for it to be a predicate following a predicate. End of quote. What I choose is that "tanzil" is a subject, "la rayba" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), and "min rabbi al-'alamin" is the predicate.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Min rabbi al-'alamin" is connected to "tanzil," so there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the sentence. It is also permissible for it to be connected to his statement "la rayba," meaning: there is no doubt from the side of Allah, the Exalted; and if the disbelievers doubt, that is not taken into account. "Al-rayb" means doubt, and so it is in the whole Qur'an, except His statement ﴿the vicissitudes of fate﴾ [al-Tur 30]. End of quote.

When "tanzil" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a parenthetical insertion between what requires something else and what it requires, we do not say there is inversion in it; rather, if it were placed later it would not be a parenthetical insertion. As for it being connected to "la rayba," that is not good, because the negation of doubt from it absolutely is the intended meaning. The meaning is: there is no room for doubt in it, that it is the revelation of Allah, because the reason for negating doubt about it is present in it, which is its inimitability (i'jaz), so it is the furthest thing from doubt. Their statement "He fabricated it" is the speech of an ignorant person who did not reflect carefully, or of a denier who is certain that it is from Allah, and so says that out of envy, or it is a judgment from Allah upon him with misguidance.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the content of the sentence, as if it were said: there is no doubt about that, meaning, about its being sent down from the Lord of the worlds. What supports its soundness is His statement ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"﴾, because their saying "this is fabricated" is a denial that it could be from the Lord of the worlds. Likewise His statement ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, and what is in it of an implication that it is from Allah. This is a sound and firm style: He first established that its sending down is from the Lord of the worlds, and that this is what there is no doubt about. Then He turned away from that to His statement "Or do they say, 'He has fabricated it'", because "am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather), and the interrogative hamza is for denial of their statement and for amazement at it, since its matter is clear in the incapacity of their eloquent people to produce the like of even three verses. Then He turned from denial to affirmation: that it is the truth from your Lord. End of quote, and it is a statement that contains excess.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Am" may mean "bal yaqulun" (rather they say), so it is a shift from one topic to another. "Min rabbika" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: existing from the side of your Lord. Its connection is to "li-tundhira" (that you may warn), or to an omitted element whose estimate is: He sent it down so that you may warn. The people here are Quraysh and the Arabs. "Ma" is a negation particle, and "min nadhir" has "min" as an extra particle, and "nadhir" is the subject (fa'il) of "ataham."

He (exalted is He) informed that He did not send a messenger to them specifically before Muhammad, neither to them nor to their fathers; but they were worshipping according to the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, and they continued upon that until some of their leaders changed that, worshipped idols, and that became general. So they fall under His statement ﴿And there is no community but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], meaning: its law and its religion. The warner is not restricted to one who directly reached them, but is a warner for whoever he directly reached, and for others nearby to whom a warner had come before. No warner directly reached them other than Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: the meaning is that no warner came to them in the interval (fatrah) between 'Isa and Muhammad, upon them both be peace.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What no warner had come to them from before you" is like His statement ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ [Ya-Sin 6]. That is because Quraysh, Allah did not send a messenger to them before Muhammad. If you say: then if no warner came to them, the proof was not established against them. I say: as for the establishment of proof through the laws whose knowledge can be reached only through messengers, no; but as for its establishment through knowledge of Allah, His tawhid and His wisdom, yes, because the proofs of reason leading to that were with them in every age. End of quote.

What has been adopted is not what the commentators adopted. They understood from His statement "what there had not come to them" and "what their fathers were not warned" that "ma" is a negation particle. In my view "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the meaning is: that you may warn a people of the punishment that has come to them. "Min nadhir" is connected to "ataham" (has come to them), meaning: came to them through a warner from before you. Likewise ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were warned﴾ [Ya-Sin 6], meaning the punishment their fathers were warned of. So "ma" is the object in both places, and "unzira" (was warned) takes two objects. He (exalted is He) said: ﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt"﴾ [Fussilat 13]. This statement is in accordance with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And there is no community but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]; and ﴿lest you should say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings or warner." But there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah 19]; ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15]; ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother a messenger﴾ [al-Qasas 59].

When He (exalted is He) related from them that they say Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricated it, and refuted them, He limited what the Qur'an brought to warning, although it had also brought good tidings, so that this would be a deterrent for them. And because when warning is mentioned, a thinking person reflects on what he is warned of, and perhaps that reflection will be a cause of his guidance. The statement "la'allahum yahtadun" (perhaps they will be guided) is an expression of hope from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as in His statement ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha 44], addressed to Musa and Harun. Al-Zamakhshari said: The word of hope (tarajji) is used metaphorically for will (irada). End of quote. He means that he expressed will by the word of hope, and its meaning is the will for their guidance. This is a Mu'tazili tendency (al-I'tizaliyyah), because according to them, Allah wills the guidance of the servant, yet what He wills does not occur, and what the servant wills occurs. Exalted is Allah above that.

When He (exalted is He) clarified the matter of the message, He mentioned what is incumbent upon the Messenger (ﷺ) of calling to tawhid, and establishing the proof by mentioning the origin of the world. The discussion of ﴿in six days﴾ [al-A'raf 54] has preceded in al-A'raf.

﴿You have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾: meaning, if you go beyond Him to other than Him, you take it as a helper and intercessor. "Will you not then remember" the Originator of this world, so that you worship Him and abandon what is other than Him?

"He arranges the affair": "al-amr" is the singular of "al-umur" (affairs). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: Allah executes His decree with all that He wills.

﴿Then it ascends to Him﴾: meaning it rises. This is the predicate of that. "In a day" is one of the days of the world, "its measure" being what it would be if traversed by the normal pace of humans, "a thousand years," because the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years. Mujahid also said: the pronoun in "its measure" refers to the arrangement (tadbir), meaning the measure of the arrangement that is completed in a day would be a thousand years if humans arranged it. Mujahid also said: He arranges and delivers to the angels the matters of a thousand years from Our side, and that is one day with Him; when it is finished, He delivers its like to them. So the meaning is that affairs are executed from Him for this period and ultimately return to Him, because the final outcome of affairs is to Him. It was also said: the meaning is that He arranges it in this world until the Hour is established, then the decree and destiny descend, and then it ascends to Him on the Day of Resurrection; its measure is what has been mentioned, so that He may judge in that day, when the command of rulers and the judgments of judges cease, and He alone holds command. Each day of the Hereafter is a thousand years, and for the disbelievers it is the measure of fifty thousand years, as in the surah "A questioner asked" (al-Ma'arij), and the opinions about it will come, God willing. It was also said: the Revelation descends with Gabriel from the heaven to the earth, then returns to what it was, accepting the revelation, or to its Lord with Gabriel; and that is in a time which in reality is a thousand years, because the distance, going down and coming up, is a journey of a thousand years, since the distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of five hundred years; and it is a day of your days owing to the speed of Gabriel, because he covers a journey of a thousand years in one day. Al-Zamakhshari said: The beginning of the matter commanded, of acts of obedience and righteous deeds, He sends down arranged from the heaven to the earth, then it is not acted upon, and that commanded matter does not ascend to Him purely as He wills and approves, except after a lengthy period, because of the scarcity of deeds for Allah and sincerity from His servants, and the scarcity of ascending deeds; for only the pure is described as ascending. This is indicated by His statement following it: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾. End of quote.

It is said: He directs the affair of the sun in its rising from the east and its setting in the west, and its course in the world from the heaven to the earth; for it rises over the people of the earth until it sets, and returns to its place of rising, in a day whose measure in distance is a thousand years. The pronoun in (ilayhi) refers to the heaven, because it is masculine in meaning [lit. "because it is referred to in the masculine"]; and it is said that it refers to God. ʿAbdullah ibn Sabit said: Four direct the affair of the world: Jibril for the winds, the hosts and Mikail for rain and water, the Angel of Death for taking souls, and Israfil for the descent of the command upon them. It is also said: the Throne is the place of direction, what is below it is the place of detailing, and what is below the heavens is the place of making known. As-Suddi said: "the command" is the revelation. Muqatil said: the decree. Others said: the affair of the world. Az-Zajjaj said: you say ʿarraja fi as-sullam, aʿruju ("I climbed the ladder"), and ʿaraja ar-rajul yaʿruju when he became lame. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read (yaʿruju) in the passive voice; the majority read it in the active voice. Abu ʿAbdullah ar-Razi said: In this there is a subtle point, namely that God mentioned in the previous verse the world of bodies and creation, and pointed to the greatness of the dominion; and here He mentions the world of spirits and the command with His words "He directs the command," and the spirit is from the world of command, as He said: ﴿Say: the spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra: 85]; and He pointed to its permanence with a expression that suggests time. What is meant is the permanence of endurance, as it is said in common usage: "the time of so-and-so has lengthened," and time extends and is found in many times. So He pointed to the greatness of the dominion by place, and pointed to its permanence here by time and place from His creation and dominion, and time by His judgment and command. End. And this is a statement that does not run according to the understanding of the Arabs. The majority read (mimma taʿuddun) with the ta of address; as-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash and al-Hasan read it with the ya of the third person, with a variant reported from al-Hasan. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read: "thumma taʿruju al-malaikatu," with the addition of "al-malaikah," and perhaps this was an explanation by him of its omission in the body of the Mushaf.

(Dhalika) i.e., that One described with creation, establishment and direction, (ʿalim al-ghayb) — the unseen — and the unseen is the Hereafter, (wa-sh-shahada) — the witnessed — the present world; or the unseen is what is hidden from creatures, and the witnessed is what is seen of things; these are two opinions. Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿ʿālimi al-ghaybi wa-sh-shahādati al-ʿazīzi ar-raḥīmi﴾ with the three attributes in the genitive; and Abu Zayd an-Nahwi (read) with the genitive of "al-ʿazizi ar-rahimi." The majority read the three in the nominative, either as predicates of that, or the first is a predicate and the two others are attributes. The reason for the genitive is that dhalika refers to the command, and it is the subject of (yaʿruju), meaning: then that [command] ascends to Him, i.e., the directed command, and "ʿalimi" and what follows are a substitute for the pronoun in "ilayhi." In the reading of Ibn Zayd, (dhalika ʿalimu) is a subject and predicate, and "al-ʿazizi ar-rahimi" in the genitive is a substitute for the pronoun in "ilayhi."

The majority read (khalaqahu), with a fatha on the lam, as a past verb, an attribute of (kulla) or of (shayʾin). The two Arab readers (Abu ʿAmr and Nafiʿ? [as the text says "al-ʿarabiyyan"]) and Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the lam; the apparent reading is that it is a substitute of inclusion, and the substituted-from is "kull", i.e., the best creation of every thing, so the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to (kull). It is also said that the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to God, so its accusative is the accusative of a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the sentence, like His words ﴿the dye of God﴾ [al-Baqara: 138], and this is the view of Sibawayh, i.e., He created it as a creation. He preferred this over the substitute of inclusion because it involves the verbal noun being attached to the agent, which is more common than attaching it to the object, and because it is more eloquent in showing favor; for when He says ﴿who made well everything﴾ it is more eloquent than "who made well the creation of everything," since one may make a creation well while the thing itself is not good in itself; but when He says ﴿made well everything﴾ it implies that everything He created is good, in the sense that He placed everything in its proper place. End.

It is also said: in this view, namely that the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to God, it is a substitute of "kull shayʾin" — a substitute of a thing from a thing, and both are for one referent. The meaning of (ahsana) is "made good," because there is nothing He created that is not arranged according to what wisdom requires. Thus all created things are good, though they vary in goodness, and their goodness is from the perspective of the purpose for which they were intended. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas said: monkeys are not good-looking, but they are well-made and firmly constructed. On the reading of those who made the lam of (khalaqahu) quiescent, Mujahid said: He gave every kind its form, and the meaning: every thing was created in the form specific to it. Al-Farra said: He inspired every thing with its creation in what they need, as if He informed them of it, so it is like His words ﴿gave every thing its creation﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50].

The majority read (badaʾa) with a hamza; az-Zuhri read it with an alif in place of the hamza. It is not regular to say, of hadaʾa, "hada," by replacing the hamza with an alif; rather the regular treatment of this hamza is facilitation between-between (tahqiq bayn bayn); though al-Akhfash reported "qaraʾtu" → "qaraytu" and similar. It is also said that it is a dialectal form; the Ansar say, for badaʾa, "badiya," with the kasra of the middle radical and a ya after it, which is a dialect of Tayyi'; they say for fa'ila like baqiya: baqaʾa; so it is possible that az-Zuhri's reading is on this dialect, its origin being badiya, then it became bada, or on the dialect of the Ansar. Ibn Rawaha said:

*By the name of God and by Him we began, and had we worshipped other than Him we would have been wretched.*

﴿And He began the creation of man﴾ — he is Adam, peace be upon him.
﴿Then He made his offspring﴾ — i.e., his descendants. "Nasala min ash-shayʾ": it separated from it.
﴿Then He fashioned him﴾ — He made him upright; and He attributed the spirit to His own self, as an indication that it is a wondrous creation, whose reality none knows but Him; and this is the attribution of a possession to its owner and of a creation to its Creator, exalted is He. (Wa-jaʿala lakum) is a shift (iltifat), for it is a move from a singular absent pronoun to a plural addressed one, and an enumeration of blessings; and it includes Adam, just as the fashioning and breathing of the spirit includes him and his descendants. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (wa-qalu) refers to a plural; it is said the speaker was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it is attributed to the plural because they approved of it. The verb governing the adverb is omitted, indicated by (aʾinna) and what follows, its estimated form being "was raised."

﴿Are we, when we have gone astray﴾ — and whoever reads "idha" without the interrogative, then the answer of idha is omitted, i.e., "when we have gone astray in the earth we will be raised," and it is a statement from them by way of mockery. Likewise whoever reads "inna" as a declarative, they doubled that mockery with another mockery. The majority read the lam with a fatha, and the present form "yadillu" with a kasra on the middle radical, which is the famous and eloquent dialect, the dialect of Najd. Mujahid said: "we perished"; every thing that is overcome by another until it is lost and hidden has perished, and its origin is from "dalla al-ma' fi al-laban," when it vanished. Qutrub said: "dalalna" means: we were hidden in the earth, and he recited the verse of an-Nabigha adh-Dhubyani:

*So the ones who hid him returned with a clear sign, and Hazm and Na'il were left behind at al-Jawlan.*

Yahya ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Rajaʾ, Talha and Ibn Wathhab read the lam with a kasra, and the present with a fatha; this is the dialect of Abu al-ʿAliya. Abu Haywa read "dulilna" with a dotted dad, its damma, and the lam kasra with shadda, reported from ʿAli. ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and Aban ibn Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs read "salalna" with an undotted sad and a fatha on the lam, meaning: we became putrid. And from al-Hasan: "salilna," with a kasra on the lam; it is said: salla yasillu, with a fatha on the middle radical in the past and a kasra in the present; salla yasallu, with a kasra in the past and a fatha in the present; and aSalla yasillu, with a hamza, on the pattern af'ala. The poet said:

*She chews a morsel, in which is a rot; it has become rotten, and beneath the flank is a disease.*

Al-Farra said: its meaning is we became in the hard dry earth (ṣalla). An-Nahhas said: we do not know "salalna" in the language, but it is said: aSalla al-lahm and Salla, and akhamma and khamma, when it stank; others have reported it.

﴿Nay, they are, in meeting their Lord, disbelievers﴾ — deniers of the meeting with God and of the arrival at His recompense. Then God commanded him to inform them of the general state, not in detail, of the seizing of their souls, then their return to their Lord's recompense through resurrection. ﴿The Angel of Death﴾ — his name is ʿIzrail, and its meaning is "servant of God." The majority read (turjaʿun) in the passive voice; Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the active.

(Wa-law tara) — the apparent reading is that it is an address to the Messenger; it is said: to him and to his community; i.e., "and if you could see, O Muhammad, those who deny resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would see a wonder." Abu al-ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: "O Muhammad, say to the criminal: (and if you could see)." He saw that the clause is conjoined to (yatawaffakum) within the scope of (qul), and therefore he did not make it an address to the Messenger. The apparent reading is that "law" here has not taken on the sense of wishing; rather it is the one for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else, and the answer is omitted, i.e., "you would have seen the worst state that could be seen." "Law" here is a conditional for the past, and "idh" is a time-adverb for the past; for the certainty of the report and its occurrence, they are used together, placing it in the position of the past. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it is an address to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and in this there are two views: the first, that it means wishing, as if it were said: "would that you could see"; the wishing is for him, just as hope was for him in (perhaps they will be guided), because he endured from them the choking and their enmity and harm; so God granted him the wish to see them in that horrible state of shame, disgrace and grief, so that he might take pleasure at their expense; and the second, that "law" is counterfactual, and its answer has been omitted, namely: "you would have seen a dreadful matter." It is also permissible that anyone be addressed by it, as you say: "So-and-so is base: if you honor him he insults you, and if you do good to him he harms you," so you do not mean a specific addressee; it is as if you said: "if he is honored, and if he is done good." End. The wishing sense of "law" in this place is far-fetched, and calling "law" counterfactual is not good; rather the correct expression is: "law" for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else, which is Sibawayh's expression. His saying the answer has been omitted, with its estimate "would that you could see what shows that it was then for wishing, has no answer," but the correct view is that when it is infused with the sense of wishing it has an answer, just as its state when not infused. The poet said:

*Even if the graves were dug up for Kulayb, and he were asked which of the Dhana'ib...*
*On the day of Ash-Sha'thamayn he would have consoled an eye; and how is meeting one who is under the graves?*

Az-Zamakhshari also said: "law" may come in the sense of wishing, as in your saying: "law you came to me and told me," just as you say: "would that you came to me and told me." Ibn Malik said: if he meant that it is omitted, i.e., "I wished that you would come to me," then it is correct; but if he meant that it is set for wishing, then it is not correct, for if it were set for it, it could not be combined with the verb of wishing; one cannot say "I wished would you do," though one may say "I wished law you stood." Likewise, the combination of "la'alla" with hope, and of "illa" with "astathni" is impossible. End.

﴿Bowing their heads﴾ — lowering them, from humiliation, sorrow, distress, grief and blame. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "nakkasu ruʾusahum," as a past verb with an object; the majority read it as an active participle with an object. (ʿInda rabbihim) — i.e., at His requital, which is a place of extreme shame, for the one who is nurtured, when he has done wrong and stands before his Lord, is in utmost embarrassment. (Rabbana) — with the implied "they say"; az-Zamakhshari estimated it as: they cry out for help with their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen﴾ what we used to deny; ﴿and we have heard﴾ what we used to reject; and we have seen the truth of Your promise and Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers; and we were blind and deaf, but now we have seen and heard, so send us back to the world.

"Indeed we are certain" (inna muqinun): that is, of the resurrection. This was said by al-Naqqash. It was also said: "We are those who affirm the truth of what the Messenger ﷺ said," as related from Yahya ibn Salam.

"Muqinun" implies a state of having become certain at this moment, that is, when they see and hear. It was also said: the doubts have now been removed from us; we did not reflect in the world, and we were like those who neither see nor hear. It was also said: "To You belongs the proof, our Lord; we have now seen Your messengers and wonders in the world, and heard their speech, so we have no proof left for ourselves." This is a confession from them.

(p-196) This surah is Meccan. It was said that five verses are an exception: from ﴿They forsake their beds﴾ [al-Sajdah 16] to "you used to deny" (tukadhdhibun). Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said that three verses were revealed at Medina: ﴿Is one who was a believer﴾ [al-Sajdah 18]. The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Allah did not send Muhammad to us, and what he brought is only his own fabrication." So this was revealed. Since, before this, He (exalted is He) mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God) from the beginning of creation, which is the first principle, and then mentioned the resurrection and the gathering, which is the second principle, and closed the surah with it, He mentioned at the beginning of this surah the third principle, which is the clarification of the message (risalah).

"Al-Kitab" means the Qur'an. Al-Hufi said: "Tanzil" is a subject (mubtada'), and "la rayba" is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for "tanzil" to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this recited text is a revelation (tanzil), or these letters are a revelation, and "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a substitution (badal) for the letters. Abu al-Baqa' said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a subject, and "tanzil" is its predicate in the sense of "mazil" (a sent-down thing); "la rayba fihi" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "al-Kitab," and the governing element in it is "tanzil"; and "min rabbi al-'alamin" is also connected to "tanzil." It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "fihi," and the governing element in it is the adverbial phrase. It is also permissible for "tanzil" to be a subject, with "la rayba fihi" as the predicate, and "min rabbi al-'alamin" a circumstantial clause, as previously mentioned. It is not permissible on this view for it to be connected to "tanzil," because the verbal noun has already been given as a predicate. It is also permissible for the predicate to be "min rabbi al-'alamin," with "la rayba" a circumstantial clause from "al-Kitab," and for it to be a predicate following a predicate. End of quote. What I choose is that "tanzil" is a subject, "la rayba" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), and "min rabbi al-'alamin" is the predicate.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Min rabbi al-'alamin" is connected to "tanzil," so there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the sentence. It is also permissible for it to be connected to his statement "la rayba," meaning: there is no doubt from the side of Allah, the Exalted; and if the disbelievers doubt, that is not taken into account. "Al-rayb" means doubt, and so it is in the whole Qur'an, except His statement ﴿the vicissitudes of fate﴾ [al-Tur 30]. End of quote.

When "tanzil" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a parenthetical insertion between what requires something else and what it requires, we do not say there is inversion in it; rather, if it were placed later it would not be a parenthetical insertion. As for it being connected to "la rayba," that is not good, because the negation of doubt from it absolutely is the intended meaning. The meaning is: there is no room for doubt in it, that it is the revelation of Allah, because the reason for negating doubt about it is present in it, which is its inimitability (i'jaz), so it is the furthest thing from doubt. Their statement "He fabricated it" is the speech of an ignorant person who did not reflect carefully, or of a denier who is certain that it is from Allah, and so says that out of envy, or it is a judgment from Allah upon him with misguidance.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the content of the sentence, as if it were said: there is no doubt about that, meaning, about its being sent down from the Lord of the worlds. What supports its soundness is His statement ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"﴾, because their saying "this is fabricated" is a denial that it could be from the Lord of the worlds. Likewise His statement ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, and what is in it of an implication that it is from Allah. This is a sound and firm style: He first established that its sending down is from the Lord of the worlds, and that this is what there is no doubt about. Then He turned away from that to His statement "Or do they say, 'He has fabricated it'", because "am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather), and the interrogative hamza is for denial of their statement and for amazement at it, since its matter is clear in the incapacity of their eloquent people to produce the like of even three verses. Then He turned from denial to affirmation: that it is the truth from your Lord. End of quote, and it is a statement that contains excess.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Am" may mean "bal yaqulun" (rather they say), so it is a shift from one topic to another. "Min rabbika" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: existing from the side of your Lord. Its connection is to "li-tundhira" (that you may warn), or to an omitted element whose estimate is: He sent it down so that you may warn. The people here are Quraysh and the Arabs. "Ma" is a negation particle, and "min nadhir" has "min" as an extra particle, and "nadhir" is the subject (fa'il) of "ataham."

He (exalted is He) informed that He did not send a messenger to them specifically before Muhammad, neither to them nor to their fathers; but they were worshipping according to the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, and they continued upon that until some of their leaders changed that, worshipped idols, and that became general. So they fall under His statement ﴿And there is no community but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], meaning: its law and its religion. The warner is not restricted to one who directly reached them, but is a warner for whoever he directly reached, and for others nearby to whom a warner had come before. No warner directly reached them other than Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: the meaning is that no warner came to them in the interval (fatrah) between 'Isa and Muhammad, upon them both be peace.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What no warner had come to them from before you" is like His statement ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ [Ya-Sin 6]. That is because Quraysh, Allah did not send a messenger to them before Muhammad. If you say: then if no warner came to them, the proof was not established against them. I say: as for the establishment of proof through the laws whose knowledge can be reached only through messengers, no; but as for its establishment through knowledge of Allah, His tawhid and His wisdom, yes, because the proofs of reason leading to that were with them in every age. End of quote.

What has been adopted is not what the commentators adopted. They understood from His statement "what there had not come to them" and "what their fathers were not warned" that "ma" is a negation particle. In my view "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the meaning is: that you may warn a people of the punishment that has come to them. "Min nadhir" is connected to "ataham" (has come to them), meaning: came to them through a warner from before you. Likewise ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were warned﴾ [Ya-Sin 6], meaning the punishment their fathers were warned of. So "ma" is the object in both places, and "unzira" (was warned) takes two objects. He (exalted is He) said: ﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt"﴾ [Fussilat 13]. This statement is in accordance with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And there is no community but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]; and ﴿lest you should say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings or warner." But there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah 19]; ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15]; ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother a messenger﴾ [al-Qasas 59].

When He (exalted is He) related from them that they say Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricated it, and refuted them, He limited what the Qur'an brought to warning, although it had also brought good tidings, so that this would be a deterrent for them. And because when warning is mentioned, a thinking person reflects on what he is warned of, and perhaps that reflection will be a cause of his guidance. The statement "la'allahum yahtadun" (perhaps they will be guided) is an expression of hope from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as in His statement ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha 44], addressed to Musa and Harun. Al-Zamakhshari said: The word of hope (tarajji) is used metaphorically for will (irada). End of quote. He means that he expressed will by the word of hope, and its meaning is the will for their guidance. This is a Mu'tazili tendency (al-I'tizaliyyah), because according to them, Allah wills the guidance of the servant, yet what He wills does not occur, and what the servant wills occurs. Exalted is Allah above that.

When He (exalted is He) clarified the matter of the message, He mentioned what is incumbent upon the Messenger (ﷺ) of calling to tawhid, and establishing the proof by mentioning the origin of the world. The discussion of ﴿in six days﴾ [al-A'raf 54] has preceded in al-A'raf.

﴿You have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾: meaning, if you go beyond Him to other than Him, you take it as a helper and intercessor. "Will you not then remember" the Originator of this world, so that you worship Him and abandon what is other than Him?

"He arranges the affair": "al-amr" is the singular of "al-umur" (affairs). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: Allah executes His decree with all that He wills.

﴿Then it ascends to Him﴾: meaning it rises. This is the predicate of that. "In a day" is one of the days of the world, "its measure" being what it would be if traversed by the normal pace of humans, "a thousand years," because the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years. Mujahid also said: the pronoun in "its measure" refers to the arrangement (tadbir), meaning the measure of the arrangement that is completed in a day would be a thousand years if humans arranged it. Mujahid also said: He arranges and delivers to the angels the matters of a thousand years from Our side, and that is one day with Him; when it is finished, He delivers its like to them. So the meaning is that affairs are executed from Him for this period and ultimately return to Him, because the final outcome of affairs is to Him. It was also said: the meaning is that He arranges it in this world until the Hour is established, then the decree and destiny descend, and then it ascends to Him on the Day of Resurrection; its measure is what has been mentioned, so that He may judge in that day, when the command of rulers and the judgments of judges cease, and He alone holds command. Each day of the Hereafter is a thousand years, and for the disbelievers it is the measure of fifty thousand years, as in the surah "A questioner asked" (al-Ma'arij), and the opinions about it will come, God willing. It was also said: the Revelation descends with Gabriel from the heaven to the earth, then returns to what it was, accepting the revelation, or to its Lord with Gabriel; and that is in a time which in reality is a thousand years, because the distance, going down and coming up, is a journey of a thousand years, since the distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of five hundred years; and it is a day of your days owing to the speed of Gabriel, because he covers a journey of a thousand years in one day. Al-Zamakhshari said: The beginning of the matter commanded, of acts of obedience and righteous deeds, He sends down arranged from the heaven to the earth, then it is not acted upon, and that commanded matter does not ascend to Him purely as He wills and approves, except after a lengthy period, because of the scarcity of deeds for Allah and sincerity from His servants, and the scarcity of ascending deeds; for only the pure is described as ascending. This is indicated by His statement following it: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾. End of quote.

It is said: He directs the affair of the sun in its rising from the east and its setting in the west, and its course in the world from the heaven to the earth; for it rises over the people of the earth until it sets, and returns to its place of rising, in a day whose measure in distance is a thousand years. The pronoun in (ilayhi) refers to the heaven, because it is masculine in meaning [lit. "because it is referred to in the masculine"]; and it is said that it refers to God. ʿAbdullah ibn Sabit said: Four direct the affair of the world: Jibril for the winds, the hosts and Mikail for rain and water, the Angel of Death for taking souls, and Israfil for the descent of the command upon them. It is also said: the Throne is the place of direction, what is below it is the place of detailing, and what is below the heavens is the place of making known. As-Suddi said: "the command" is the revelation. Muqatil said: the decree. Others said: the affair of the world. Az-Zajjaj said: you say ʿarraja fi as-sullam, aʿruju ("I climbed the ladder"), and ʿaraja ar-rajul yaʿruju when he became lame. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read (yaʿruju) in the passive voice; the majority read it in the active voice. Abu ʿAbdullah ar-Razi said: In this there is a subtle point, namely that God mentioned in the previous verse the world of bodies and creation, and pointed to the greatness of the dominion; and here He mentions the world of spirits and the command with His words "He directs the command," and the spirit is from the world of command, as He said: ﴿Say: the spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra: 85]; and He pointed to its permanence with a expression that suggests time. What is meant is the permanence of endurance, as it is said in common usage: "the time of so-and-so has lengthened," and time extends and is found in many times. So He pointed to the greatness of the dominion by place, and pointed to its permanence here by time and place from His creation and dominion, and time by His judgment and command. End. And this is a statement that does not run according to the understanding of the Arabs. The majority read (mimma taʿuddun) with the ta of address; as-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash and al-Hasan read it with the ya of the third person, with a variant reported from al-Hasan. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read: "thumma taʿruju al-malaikatu," with the addition of "al-malaikah," and perhaps this was an explanation by him of its omission in the body of the Mushaf.

(Dhalika) i.e., that One described with creation, establishment and direction, (ʿalim al-ghayb) — the unseen — and the unseen is the Hereafter, (wa-sh-shahada) — the witnessed — the present world; or the unseen is what is hidden from creatures, and the witnessed is what is seen of things; these are two opinions. Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿ʿālimi al-ghaybi wa-sh-shahādati al-ʿazīzi ar-raḥīmi﴾ with the three attributes in the genitive; and Abu Zayd an-Nahwi (read) with the genitive of "al-ʿazizi ar-rahimi." The majority read the three in the nominative, either as predicates of that, or the first is a predicate and the two others are attributes. The reason for the genitive is that dhalika refers to the command, and it is the subject of (yaʿruju), meaning: then that [command] ascends to Him, i.e., the directed command, and "ʿalimi" and what follows are a substitute for the pronoun in "ilayhi." In the reading of Ibn Zayd, (dhalika ʿalimu) is a subject and predicate, and "al-ʿazizi ar-rahimi" in the genitive is a substitute for the pronoun in "ilayhi."

The majority read (khalaqahu), with a fatha on the lam, as a past verb, an attribute of (kulla) or of (shayʾin). The two Arab readers (Abu ʿAmr and Nafiʿ? [as the text says "al-ʿarabiyyan"]) and Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the lam; the apparent reading is that it is a substitute of inclusion, and the substituted-from is "kull", i.e., the best creation of every thing, so the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to (kull). It is also said that the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to God, so its accusative is the accusative of a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the sentence, like His words ﴿the dye of God﴾ [al-Baqara: 138], and this is the view of Sibawayh, i.e., He created it as a creation. He preferred this over the substitute of inclusion because it involves the verbal noun being attached to the agent, which is more common than attaching it to the object, and because it is more eloquent in showing favor; for when He says ﴿who made well everything﴾ it is more eloquent than "who made well the creation of everything," since one may make a creation well while the thing itself is not good in itself; but when He says ﴿made well everything﴾ it implies that everything He created is good, in the sense that He placed everything in its proper place. End.

It is also said: in this view, namely that the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to God, it is a substitute of "kull shayʾin" — a substitute of a thing from a thing, and both are for one referent. The meaning of (ahsana) is "made good," because there is nothing He created that is not arranged according to what wisdom requires. Thus all created things are good, though they vary in goodness, and their goodness is from the perspective of the purpose for which they were intended. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas said: monkeys are not good-looking, but they are well-made and firmly constructed. On the reading of those who made the lam of (khalaqahu) quiescent, Mujahid said: He gave every kind its form, and the meaning: every thing was created in the form specific to it. Al-Farra said: He inspired every thing with its creation in what they need, as if He informed them of it, so it is like His words ﴿gave every thing its creation﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50].

The majority read (badaʾa) with a hamza; az-Zuhri read it with an alif in place of the hamza. It is not regular to say, of hadaʾa, "hada," by replacing the hamza with an alif; rather the regular treatment of this hamza is facilitation between-between (tahqiq bayn bayn); though al-Akhfash reported "qaraʾtu" → "qaraytu" and similar. It is also said that it is a dialectal form; the Ansar say, for badaʾa, "badiya," with the kasra of the middle radical and a ya after it, which is a dialect of Tayyi'; they say for fa'ila like baqiya: baqaʾa; so it is possible that az-Zuhri's reading is on this dialect, its origin being badiya, then it became bada, or on the dialect of the Ansar. Ibn Rawaha said:

*By the name of God and by Him we began, and had we worshipped other than Him we would have been wretched.*

﴿And He began the creation of man﴾ — he is Adam, peace be upon him.
﴿Then He made his offspring﴾ — i.e., his descendants. "Nasala min ash-shayʾ": it separated from it.
﴿Then He fashioned him﴾ — He made him upright; and He attributed the spirit to His own self, as an indication that it is a wondrous creation, whose reality none knows but Him; and this is the attribution of a possession to its owner and of a creation to its Creator, exalted is He. (Wa-jaʿala lakum) is a shift (iltifat), for it is a move from a singular absent pronoun to a plural addressed one, and an enumeration of blessings; and it includes Adam, just as the fashioning and breathing of the spirit includes him and his descendants. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (wa-qalu) refers to a plural; it is said the speaker was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it is attributed to the plural because they approved of it. The verb governing the adverb is omitted, indicated by (aʾinna) and what follows, its estimated form being "was raised."

﴿Are we, when we have gone astray﴾ — and whoever reads "idha" without the interrogative, then the answer of idha is omitted, i.e., "when we have gone astray in the earth we will be raised," and it is a statement from them by way of mockery. Likewise whoever reads "inna" as a declarative, they doubled that mockery with another mockery. The majority read the lam with a fatha, and the present form "yadillu" with a kasra on the middle radical, which is the famous and eloquent dialect, the dialect of Najd. Mujahid said: "we perished"; every thing that is overcome by another until it is lost and hidden has perished, and its origin is from "dalla al-ma' fi al-laban," when it vanished. Qutrub said: "dalalna" means: we were hidden in the earth, and he recited the verse of an-Nabigha adh-Dhubyani:

*So the ones who hid him returned with a clear sign, and Hazm and Na'il were left behind at al-Jawlan.*

Yahya ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Rajaʾ, Talha and Ibn Wathhab read the lam with a kasra, and the present with a fatha; this is the dialect of Abu al-ʿAliya. Abu Haywa read "dulilna" with a dotted dad, its damma, and the lam kasra with shadda, reported from ʿAli. ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and Aban ibn Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs read "salalna" with an undotted sad and a fatha on the lam, meaning: we became putrid. And from al-Hasan: "salilna," with a kasra on the lam; it is said: salla yasillu, with a fatha on the middle radical in the past and a kasra in the present; salla yasallu, with a kasra in the past and a fatha in the present; and aSalla yasillu, with a hamza, on the pattern af'ala. The poet said:

*She chews a morsel, in which is a rot; it has become rotten, and beneath the flank is a disease.*

Al-Farra said: its meaning is we became in the hard dry earth (ṣalla). An-Nahhas said: we do not know "salalna" in the language, but it is said: aSalla al-lahm and Salla, and akhamma and khamma, when it stank; others have reported it.

﴿Nay, they are, in meeting their Lord, disbelievers﴾ — deniers of the meeting with God and of the arrival at His recompense. Then God commanded him to inform them of the general state, not in detail, of the seizing of their souls, then their return to their Lord's recompense through resurrection. ﴿The Angel of Death﴾ — his name is ʿIzrail, and its meaning is "servant of God." The majority read (turjaʿun) in the passive voice; Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the active.

(Wa-law tara) — the apparent reading is that it is an address to the Messenger; it is said: to him and to his community; i.e., "and if you could see, O Muhammad, those who deny resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would see a wonder." Abu al-ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: "O Muhammad, say to the criminal: (and if you could see)." He saw that the clause is conjoined to (yatawaffakum) within the scope of (qul), and therefore he did not make it an address to the Messenger. The apparent reading is that "law" here has not taken on the sense of wishing; rather it is the one for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else, and the answer is omitted, i.e., "you would have seen the worst state that could be seen." "Law" here is a conditional for the past, and "idh" is a time-adverb for the past; for the certainty of the report and its occurrence, they are used together, placing it in the position of the past. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it is an address to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and in this there are two views: the first, that it means wishing, as if it were said: "would that you could see"; the wishing is for him, just as hope was for him in (perhaps they will be guided), because he endured from them the choking and their enmity and harm; so God granted him the wish to see them in that horrible state of shame, disgrace and grief, so that he might take pleasure at their expense; and the second, that "law" is counterfactual, and its answer has been omitted, namely: "you would have seen a dreadful matter." It is also permissible that anyone be addressed by it, as you say: "So-and-so is base: if you honor him he insults you, and if you do good to him he harms you," so you do not mean a specific addressee; it is as if you said: "if he is honored, and if he is done good." End. The wishing sense of "law" in this place is far-fetched, and calling "law" counterfactual is not good; rather the correct expression is: "law" for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else, which is Sibawayh's expression. His saying the answer has been omitted, with its estimate "would that you could see what shows that it was then for wishing, has no answer," but the correct view is that when it is infused with the sense of wishing it has an answer, just as its state when not infused. The poet said:

*Even if the graves were dug up for Kulayb, and he were asked which of the Dhana'ib...*
*On the day of Ash-Sha'thamayn he would have consoled an eye; and how is meeting one who is under the graves?*

Az-Zamakhshari also said: "law" may come in the sense of wishing, as in your saying: "law you came to me and told me," just as you say: "would that you came to me and told me." Ibn Malik said: if he meant that it is omitted, i.e., "I wished that you would come to me," then it is correct; but if he meant that it is set for wishing, then it is not correct, for if it were set for it, it could not be combined with the verb of wishing; one cannot say "I wished would you do," though one may say "I wished law you stood." Likewise, the combination of "la'alla" with hope, and of "illa" with "astathni" is impossible. End.

﴿Bowing their heads﴾ — lowering them, from humiliation, sorrow, distress, grief and blame. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "nakkasu ruʾusahum," as a past verb with an object; the majority read it as an active participle with an object. (ʿInda rabbihim) — i.e., at His requital, which is a place of extreme shame, for the one who is nurtured, when he has done wrong and stands before his Lord, is in utmost embarrassment. (Rabbana) — with the implied "they say"; az-Zamakhshari estimated it as: they cry out for help with their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen﴾ what we used to deny; ﴿and we have heard﴾ what we used to reject; and we have seen the truth of Your promise and Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers; and we were blind and deaf, but now we have seen and heard, so send us back to the world.

"Indeed we are certain" (inna muqinun): that is, of the resurrection. This was said by al-Naqqash. It was also said: "We are those who affirm the truth of what the Messenger ﷺ said," as related from Yahya ibn Salam.

"Muqinun" implies a state of having become certain at this moment, that is, when they see and hear. It was also said: the doubts have now been removed from us; we did not reflect in the world, and we were like those who neither see nor hear. It was also said: "To You belongs the proof, our Lord; we have now seen Your messengers and wonders in the world, and heard their speech, so we have no proof left for ourselves." This is a confession from them.

(p-196) This surah is Meccan. It was said that five verses are an exception: from ﴿They forsake their beds﴾ [al-Sajdah 16] to "you used to deny" (tukadhdhibun). Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said that three verses were revealed at Medina: ﴿Is one who was a believer﴾ [al-Sajdah 18]. The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Allah did not send Muhammad to us, and what he brought is only his own fabrication." So this was revealed. Since, before this, He (exalted is He) mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God) from the beginning of creation, which is the first principle, and then mentioned the resurrection and the gathering, which is the second principle, and closed the surah with it, He mentioned at the beginning of this surah the third principle, which is the clarification of the message (risalah).

"Al-Kitab" means the Qur'an. Al-Hufi said: "Tanzil" is a subject (mubtada'), and "la rayba" is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for "tanzil" to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this recited text is a revelation (tanzil), or these letters are a revelation, and "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a substitution (badal) for the letters. Abu al-Baqa' said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a subject, and "tanzil" is its predicate in the sense of "mazil" (a sent-down thing); "la rayba fihi" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "al-Kitab," and the governing element in it is "tanzil"; and "min rabbi al-'alamin" is also connected to "tanzil." It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "fihi," and the governing element in it is the adverbial phrase. It is also permissible for "tanzil" to be a subject, with "la rayba fihi" as the predicate, and "min rabbi al-'alamin" a circumstantial clause, as previously mentioned. It is not permissible on this view for it to be connected to "tanzil," because the verbal noun has already been given as a predicate. It is also permissible for the predicate to be "min rabbi al-'alamin," with "la rayba" a circumstantial clause from "al-Kitab," and for it to be a predicate following a predicate. End of quote. What I choose is that "tanzil" is a subject, "la rayba" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), and "min rabbi al-'alamin" is the predicate.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Min rabbi al-'alamin" is connected to "tanzil," so there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the sentence. It is also permissible for it to be connected to his statement "la rayba," meaning: there is no doubt from the side of Allah, the Exalted; and if the disbelievers doubt, that is not taken into account. "Al-rayb" means doubt, and so it is in the whole Qur'an, except His statement ﴿the vicissitudes of fate﴾ [al-Tur 30]. End of quote.

When "tanzil" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a parenthetical insertion between what requires something else and what it requires, we do not say there is inversion in it; rather, if it were placed later it would not be a parenthetical insertion. As for it being connected to "la rayba," that is not good, because the negation of doubt from it absolutely is the intended meaning. The meaning is: there is no room for doubt in it, that it is the revelation of Allah, because the reason for negating doubt about it is present in it, which is its inimitability (i'jaz), so it is the furthest thing from doubt. Their statement "He fabricated it" is the speech of an ignorant person who did not reflect carefully, or of a denier who is certain that it is from Allah, and so says that out of envy, or it is a judgment from Allah upon him with misguidance.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the content of the sentence, as if it were said: there is no doubt about that, meaning, about its being sent down from the Lord of the worlds. What supports its soundness is His statement ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"﴾, because their saying "this is fabricated" is a denial that it could be from the Lord of the worlds. Likewise His statement ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, and what is in it of an implication that it is from Allah. This is a sound and firm style: He first established that its sending down is from the Lord of the worlds, and that this is what there is no doubt about. Then He turned away from that to His statement "Or do they say, 'He has fabricated it'", because "am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather), and the interrogative hamza is for denial of their statement and for amazement at it, since its matter is clear in the incapacity of their eloquent people to produce the like of even three verses. Then He turned from denial to affirmation: that it is the truth from your Lord. End of quote, and it is a statement that contains excess.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Am" may mean "bal yaqulun" (rather they say), so it is a shift from one topic to another. "Min rabbika" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: existing from the side of your Lord. Its connection is to "li-tundhira" (that you may warn), or to an omitted element whose estimate is: He sent it down so that you may warn. The people here are Quraysh and the Arabs. "Ma" is a negation particle, and "min nadhir" has "min" as an extra particle, and "nadhir" is the subject (fa'il) of "ataham."

He (exalted is He) informed that He did not send a messenger to them specifically before Muhammad, neither to them nor to their fathers; but they were worshipping according to the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, and they continued upon that until some of their leaders changed that, worshipped idols, and that became general. So they fall under His statement ﴿And there is no community but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], meaning: its law and its religion. The warner is not restricted to one who directly reached them, but is a warner for whoever he directly reached, and for others nearby to whom a warner had come before. No warner directly reached them other than Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: the meaning is that no warner came to them in the interval (fatrah) between 'Isa and Muhammad, upon them both be peace.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What no warner had come to them from before you" is like His statement ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ [Ya-Sin 6]. That is because Quraysh, Allah did not send a messenger to them before Muhammad. If you say: then if no warner came to them, the proof was not established against them. I say: as for the establishment of proof through the laws whose knowledge can be reached only through messengers, no; but as for its establishment through knowledge of Allah, His tawhid and His wisdom, yes, because the proofs of reason leading to that were with them in every age. End of quote.

What has been adopted is not what the commentators adopted. They understood from His statement "what there had not come to them" and "what their fathers were not warned" that "ma" is a negation particle. In my view "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the meaning is: that you may warn a people of the punishment that has come to them. "Min nadhir" is connected to "ataham" (has come to them), meaning: came to them through a warner from before you. Likewise ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were warned﴾ [Ya-Sin 6], meaning the punishment their fathers were warned of. So "ma" is the object in both places, and "unzira" (was warned) takes two objects. He (exalted is He) said: ﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt"﴾ [Fussilat 13]. This statement is in accordance with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And there is no community but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]; and ﴿lest you should say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings or warner." But there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah 19]; ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15]; ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother a messenger﴾ [al-Qasas 59].

When He (exalted is He) related from them that they say Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricated it, and refuted them, He limited what the Qur'an brought to warning, although it had also brought good tidings, so that this would be a deterrent for them. And because when warning is mentioned, a thinking person reflects on what he is warned of, and perhaps that reflection will be a cause of his guidance. The statement "la'allahum yahtadun" (perhaps they will be guided) is an expression of hope from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as in His statement ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha 44], addressed to Musa and Harun. Al-Zamakhshari said: The word of hope (tarajji) is used metaphorically for will (irada). End of quote. He means that he expressed will by the word of hope, and its meaning is the will for their guidance. This is a Mu'tazili tendency (al-I'tizaliyyah), because according to them, Allah wills the guidance of the servant, yet what He wills does not occur, and what the servant wills occurs. Exalted is Allah above that.

When He (exalted is He) clarified the matter of the message, He mentioned what is incumbent upon the Messenger (ﷺ) of calling to tawhid, and establishing the proof by mentioning the origin of the world. The discussion of ﴿in six days﴾ [al-A'raf 54] has preceded in al-A'raf.

﴿You have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾: meaning, if you go beyond Him to other than Him, you take it as a helper and intercessor. "Will you not then remember" the Originator of this world, so that you worship Him and abandon what is other than Him?

"He arranges the affair": "al-amr" is the singular of "al-umur" (affairs). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: Allah executes His decree with all that He wills.

﴿Then it ascends to Him﴾: meaning it rises. This is the predicate of that. "In a day" is one of the days of the world, "its measure" being what it would be if traversed by the normal pace of humans, "a thousand years," because the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years. Mujahid also said: the pronoun in "its measure" refers to the arrangement (tadbir), meaning the measure of the arrangement that is completed in a day would be a thousand years if humans arranged it. Mujahid also said: He arranges and delivers to the angels the matters of a thousand years from Our side, and that is one day with Him; when it is finished, He delivers its like to them. So the meaning is that affairs are executed from Him for this period and ultimately return to Him, because the final outcome of affairs is to Him. It was also said: the meaning is that He arranges it in this world until the Hour is established, then the decree and destiny descend, and then it ascends to Him on the Day of Resurrection; its measure is what has been mentioned, so that He may judge in that day, when the command of rulers and the judgments of judges cease, and He alone holds command. Each day of the Hereafter is a thousand years, and for the disbelievers it is the measure of fifty thousand years, as in the surah "A questioner asked" (al-Ma'arij), and the opinions about it will come, God willing. It was also said: the Revelation descends with Gabriel from the heaven to the earth, then returns to what it was, accepting the revelation, or to its Lord with Gabriel; and that is in a time which in reality is a thousand years, because the distance, going down and coming up, is a journey of a thousand years, since the distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of five hundred years; and it is a day of your days owing to the speed of Gabriel, because he covers a journey of a thousand years in one day. Al-Zamakhshari said: The beginning of the matter commanded, of acts of obedience and righteous deeds, He sends down arranged from the heaven to the earth, then it is not acted upon, and that commanded matter does not ascend to Him purely as He wills and approves, except after a lengthy period, because of the scarcity of deeds for Allah and sincerity from His servants, and the scarcity of ascending deeds; for only the pure is described as ascending. This is indicated by His statement following it: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾. End of quote.

It is said: He directs the affair of the sun in its rising from the east and its setting in the west, and its course in the world from the heaven to the earth; for it rises over the people of the earth until it sets, and returns to its place of rising, in a day whose measure in distance is a thousand years. The pronoun in (ilayhi) refers to the heaven, because it is masculine in meaning [lit. "because it is referred to in the masculine"]; and it is said that it refers to God. ʿAbdullah ibn Sabit said: Four direct the affair of the world: Jibril for the winds, the hosts and Mikail for rain and water, the Angel of Death for taking souls, and Israfil for the descent of the command upon them. It is also said: the Throne is the place of direction, what is below it is the place of detailing, and what is below the heavens is the place of making known. As-Suddi said: "the command" is the revelation. Muqatil said: the decree. Others said: the affair of the world. Az-Zajjaj said: you say ʿarraja fi as-sullam, aʿruju ("I climbed the ladder"), and ʿaraja ar-rajul yaʿruju when he became lame. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read (yaʿruju) in the passive voice; the majority read it in the active voice. Abu ʿAbdullah ar-Razi said: In this there is a subtle point, namely that God mentioned in the previous verse the world of bodies and creation, and pointed to the greatness of the dominion; and here He mentions the world of spirits and the command with His words "He directs the command," and the spirit is from the world of command, as He said: ﴿Say: the spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra: 85]; and He pointed to its permanence with a expression that suggests time. What is meant is the permanence of endurance, as it is said in common usage: "the time of so-and-so has lengthened," and time extends and is found in many times. So He pointed to the greatness of the dominion by place, and pointed to its permanence here by time and place from His creation and dominion, and time by His judgment and command. End. And this is a statement that does not run according to the understanding of the Arabs. The majority read (mimma taʿuddun) with the ta of address; as-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash and al-Hasan read it with the ya of the third person, with a variant reported from al-Hasan. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read: "thumma taʿruju al-malaikatu," with the addition of "al-malaikah," and perhaps this was an explanation by him of its omission in the body of the Mushaf.

(Dhalika) i.e., that One described with creation, establishment and direction, (ʿalim al-ghayb) — the unseen — and the unseen is the Hereafter, (wa-sh-shahada) — the witnessed — the present world; or the unseen is what is hidden from creatures, and the witnessed is what is seen of things; these are two opinions. Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿ʿālimi al-ghaybi wa-sh-shahādati al-ʿazīzi ar-raḥīmi﴾ with the three attributes in the genitive; and Abu Zayd an-Nahwi (read) with the genitive of "al-ʿazizi ar-rahimi." The majority read the three in the nominative, either as predicates of that, or the first is a predicate and the two others are attributes. The reason for the genitive is that dhalika refers to the command, and it is the subject of (yaʿruju), meaning: then that [command] ascends to Him, i.e., the directed command, and "ʿalimi" and what follows are a substitute for the pronoun in "ilayhi." In the reading of Ibn Zayd, (dhalika ʿalimu) is a subject and predicate, and "al-ʿazizi ar-rahimi" in the genitive is a substitute for the pronoun in "ilayhi."

The majority read (khalaqahu), with a fatha on the lam, as a past verb, an attribute of (kulla) or of (shayʾin). The two Arab readers (Abu ʿAmr and Nafiʿ? [as the text says "al-ʿarabiyyan"]) and Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the lam; the apparent reading is that it is a substitute of inclusion, and the substituted-from is "kull", i.e., the best creation of every thing, so the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to (kull). It is also said that the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to God, so its accusative is the accusative of a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the sentence, like His words ﴿the dye of God﴾ [al-Baqara: 138], and this is the view of Sibawayh, i.e., He created it as a creation. He preferred this over the substitute of inclusion because it involves the verbal noun being attached to the agent, which is more common than attaching it to the object, and because it is more eloquent in showing favor; for when He says ﴿who made well everything﴾ it is more eloquent than "who made well the creation of everything," since one may make a creation well while the thing itself is not good in itself; but when He says ﴿made well everything﴾ it implies that everything He created is good, in the sense that He placed everything in its proper place. End.

It is also said: in this view, namely that the pronoun in (khalaqahu) refers to God, it is a substitute of "kull shayʾin" — a substitute of a thing from a thing, and both are for one referent. The meaning of (ahsana) is "made good," because there is nothing He created that is not arranged according to what wisdom requires. Thus all created things are good, though they vary in goodness, and their goodness is from the perspective of the purpose for which they were intended. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas said: monkeys are not good-looking, but they are well-made and firmly constructed. On the reading of those who made the lam of (khalaqahu) quiescent, Mujahid said: He gave every kind its form, and the meaning: every thing was created in the form specific to it. Al-Farra said: He inspired every thing with its creation in what they need, as if He informed them of it, so it is like His words ﴿gave every thing its creation﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50].

The majority read (badaʾa) with a hamza; az-Zuhri read it with an alif in place of the hamza. It is not regular to say, of hadaʾa, "hada," by replacing the hamza with an alif; rather the regular treatment of this hamza is facilitation between-between (tahqiq bayn bayn); though al-Akhfash reported "qaraʾtu" → "qaraytu" and similar. It is also said that it is a dialectal form; the Ansar say, for badaʾa, "badiya," with the kasra of the middle radical and a ya after it, which is a dialect of Tayyi'; they say for fa'ila like baqiya: baqaʾa; so it is possible that az-Zuhri's reading is on this dialect, its origin being badiya, then it became bada, or on the dialect of the Ansar. Ibn Rawaha said:

*By the name of God and by Him we began, and had we worshipped other than Him we would have been wretched.*

﴿And He began the creation of man﴾ — he is Adam, peace be upon him.
﴿Then He made his offspring﴾ — i.e., his descendants. "Nasala min ash-shayʾ": it separated from it.
﴿Then He fashioned him﴾ — He made him upright; and He attributed the spirit to His own self, as an indication that it is a wondrous creation, whose reality none knows but Him; and this is the attribution of a possession to its owner and of a creation to its Creator, exalted is He. (Wa-jaʿala lakum) is a shift (iltifat), for it is a move from a singular absent pronoun to a plural addressed one, and an enumeration of blessings; and it includes Adam, just as the fashioning and breathing of the spirit includes him and his descendants. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (wa-qalu) refers to a plural; it is said the speaker was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it is attributed to the plural because they approved of it. The verb governing the adverb is omitted, indicated by (aʾinna) and what follows, its estimated form being "was raised."

﴿Are we, when we have gone astray﴾ — and whoever reads "idha" without the interrogative, then the answer of idha is omitted, i.e., "when we have gone astray in the earth we will be raised," and it is a statement from them by way of mockery. Likewise whoever reads "inna" as a declarative, they doubled that mockery with another mockery. The majority read the lam with a fatha, and the present form "yadillu" with a kasra on the middle radical, which is the famous and eloquent dialect, the dialect of Najd. Mujahid said: "we perished"; every thing that is overcome by another until it is lost and hidden has perished, and its origin is from "dalla al-ma' fi al-laban," when it vanished. Qutrub said: "dalalna" means: we were hidden in the earth, and he recited the verse of an-Nabigha adh-Dhubyani:

*So the ones who hid him returned with a clear sign, and Hazm and Na'il were left behind at al-Jawlan.*

Yahya ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Rajaʾ, Talha and Ibn Wathhab read the lam with a kasra, and the present with a fatha; this is the dialect of Abu al-ʿAliya. Abu Haywa read "dulilna" with a dotted dad, its damma, and the lam kasra with shadda, reported from ʿAli. ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and Aban ibn Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs read "salalna" with an undotted sad and a fatha on the lam, meaning: we became putrid. And from al-Hasan: "salilna," with a kasra on the lam; it is said: salla yasillu, with a fatha on the middle radical in the past and a kasra in the present; salla yasallu, with a kasra in the past and a fatha in the present; and aSalla yasillu, with a hamza, on the pattern af'ala. The poet said:

*She chews a morsel, in which is a rot; it has become rotten, and beneath the flank is a disease.*

Al-Farra said: its meaning is we became in the hard dry earth (ṣalla). An-Nahhas said: we do not know "salalna" in the language, but it is said: aSalla al-lahm and Salla, and akhamma and khamma, when it stank; others have reported it.

﴿Nay, they are, in meeting their Lord, disbelievers﴾ — deniers of the meeting with God and of the arrival at His recompense. Then God commanded him to inform them of the general state, not in detail, of the seizing of their souls, then their return to their Lord's recompense through resurrection. ﴿The Angel of Death﴾ — his name is ʿIzrail, and its meaning is "servant of God." The majority read (turjaʿun) in the passive voice; Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the active.

(Wa-law tara) — the apparent reading is that it is an address to the Messenger; it is said: to him and to his community; i.e., "and if you could see, O Muhammad, those who deny resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would see a wonder." Abu al-ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: "O Muhammad, say to the criminal: (and if you could see)." He saw that the clause is conjoined to (yatawaffakum) within the scope of (qul), and therefore he did not make it an address to the Messenger. The apparent reading is that "law" here has not taken on the sense of wishing; rather it is the one for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else, and the answer is omitted, i.e., "you would have seen the worst state that could be seen." "Law" here is a conditional for the past, and "idh" is a time-adverb for the past; for the certainty of the report and its occurrence, they are used together, placing it in the position of the past. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it is an address to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and in this there are two views: the first, that it means wishing, as if it were said: "would that you could see"; the wishing is for him, just as hope was for him in (perhaps they will be guided), because he endured from them the choking and their enmity and harm; so God granted him the wish to see them in that horrible state of shame, disgrace and grief, so that he might take pleasure at their expense; and the second, that "law" is counterfactual, and its answer has been omitted, namely: "you would have seen a dreadful matter." It is also permissible that anyone be addressed by it, as you say: "So-and-so is base: if you honor him he insults you, and if you do good to him he harms you," so you do not mean a specific addressee; it is as if you said: "if he is honored, and if he is done good." End. The wishing sense of "law" in this place is far-fetched, and calling "law" counterfactual is not good; rather the correct expression is: "law" for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else, which is Sibawayh's expression. His saying the answer has been omitted, with its estimate "would that you could see what shows that it was then for wishing, has no answer," but the correct view is that when it is infused with the sense of wishing it has an answer, just as its state when not infused. The poet said:

*Even if the graves were dug up for Kulayb, and he were asked which of the Dhana'ib...*
*On the day of Ash-Sha'thamayn he would have consoled an eye; and how is meeting one who is under the graves?*

Az-Zamakhshari also said: "law" may come in the sense of wishing, as in your saying: "law you came to me and told me," just as you say: "would that you came to me and told me."
