Az-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it is an address to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and in this there are two views: the first, that it means wishing, as if it were said: "would that you could see"; the wishing is for him, just as hope was for him in (perhaps they will be guided), because he endured from them the choking and their enmity and harm; so God granted him the wish to see them in that horrible state of shame, disgrace and grief, so that he might take pleasure at their expense; and the second, that "law" is counterfactual, and its answer has been omitted, namely: "you would have seen a dreadful matter." It is also permissible that anyone be addressed by it, as you say: "So-and-so is base: if you honor him he insults you, and if you do good to him he harms you," so you do not mean a specific addressee; it is as if you said: "if he is honored, and if he is done good." End. The wishing sense of "law" in this place is far-fetched, and calling "law" counterfactual is not good; rather the correct expression is: "law" for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else, which is Sibawayh's expression. His saying the answer has been omitted, with its estimate "would that you could see what shows that it was then for wishing, has no answer," but the correct view is that when it is infused with the sense of wishing it has an answer, just as its state when not infused. The poet said:

*Even if the graves were dug up for Kulayb, and he were asked which of the Dhana'ib...*
*On the day of Ash-Sha'thamayn he would have consoled an eye; and how is meeting one who is under the graves?*

Az-Zamakhshari also said: "law" may come in the sense of wishing, as in your saying: "law you came to me and told me," just as you say: "would that you came to me and told me." Ibn Malik said: if he meant that it is omitted, i.e., "I wished that you would come to me," then it is correct; but if he meant that it is set for wishing, then it is not correct, for if it were set for it, it could not be combined with the verb of wishing; one cannot say "I wished would you do," though one may say "I wished law you stood." Likewise, the combination of "la'alla" with hope, and of "illa" with "astathni" is impossible. End.

﴿Bowing their heads﴾ — lowering them, from humiliation, sorrow, distress, grief and blame. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "nakkasu ruʾusahum," as a past verb with an object; the majority read it as an active participle with an object. (ʿInda rabbihim) — i.e., at His requital, which is a place of extreme shame, for the one who is nurtured, when he has done wrong and stands before his Lord, is in utmost embarrassment. (Rabbana) — with the implied "they say"; az-Zamakhshari estimated it as: they cry out for help with their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen﴾ what we used to deny; ﴿and we have heard﴾ what we used to reject; and we have seen the truth of Your promise and Your threat, and we have heard the confirmation of Your messengers; and we were blind and deaf, but now we have seen and heard, so send us back to the world.

"Indeed we are certain" (inna muqinun): that is, of the resurrection. This was said by al-Naqqash. It was also said: "We are those who affirm the truth of what the Messenger ﷺ said," as related from Yahya ibn Salam.

"Muqinun" implies a state of having become certain at this moment, that is, when they see and hear. It was also said: the doubts have now been removed from us; we did not reflect in the world, and we were like those who neither see nor hear. It was also said: "To You belongs the proof, our Lord; we have now seen Your messengers and wonders in the world, and heard their speech, so we have no proof left for ourselves." This is a confession from them.

(p. 202) ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance. But the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together."﴾ ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this your Day. Indeed, We have forgotten you. Taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down prostrating and glorify the praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope, and they spend from what We have provided them.﴾ ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of the delight of the eyes, as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a sinner? They are not equal.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the Gardens of Refuge as a lodging, for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And as for those who sinned, their refuge is the Fire. Whenever they wish to leave it, they will be returned to it, and it will be said to them: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ ﴿And We will surely let them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, that perhaps they will return.﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them? Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals.﴾

﴿We would have given every soul its guidance﴾: i.e., We would have created faith in it. Compare His saying: ﴿Had God willed, He would have guided all mankind﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:31], and ﴿He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am 6:35], and ﴿He would have made mankind one community﴾ [Hud 11:118]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "[This is] by way of compulsion and coercion. But We based the matter on choice, not on necessity, so they preferred blindness over guidance, and thus the word of punishment came into effect against the people of blindness rather than the people of sight. Do you not see what He follows it with, His saying: ﴿So taste [it] for your forgetting﴾? He made the tasting of the punishment a result of their action of forgetting the outcome and their scant reflection upon it, and their neglect of preparing for it. The meaning of forgetting is the opposite of remembering; that is, the indulgence in desires exhausted you and diverted you from remembering the outcome, and it dominated you so that you forgot it. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have forgotten you﴾ by way of correspondence, meaning: We have requited you with a recompense for your forgetting. It was also said that it means abandonment; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others, meaning: you abandoned reflection upon the outcome, so We abandoned you from mercy." End of quotation. His saying "by way of compulsion and coercion" is the position of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that affirms human free will and divine justice in a particular way). The Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'ah) said: "It is permissible that He intends their guidance to the path of Paradise in the Hereafter, and He does not punish anyone; but the word from Him has come into effect that He will fill Hell, so it is not obligatory upon God to guide all of them to it. They said: rather, what is obligatory is the guidance of the infallible; as for one who has committed a sin, it is permissible for his guidance to be to the Fire as a recompense for his deeds. In the permissibility of that there is a prohibition, because they definitively hold that the intended meaning is guidance to faith." End of quotation.

﴿So taste﴾: the object of "taste" is omitted, or the object of "taste" is this punishment because of your forgetting ﴿the meeting of this your Day﴾, which is what you are in of humiliation of heads, disgrace and grief. Or: taste the everlasting punishment in Hell. The resumption with ﴿Indeed, We have forgotten you﴾ and the construction of the verb with inna and its noun indicates intensification of retribution against them.

﴿Only those believe in Our signs﴾: He, exalted is He, praised the believers in describing them with the most beautiful attribute: their prostration when reminded, their glorification, and their not being arrogant. This is contrary to the disbelievers' conduct of turning away from reminder, uttering abuse, and displaying arrogance. This prostration is one of the obligatory prostrations of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: prostration here means bowing (ruku'). It is reported from Ibn Jurayj: "the mosque is the place of bowing," meaning from this; and it follows from this that the verse is Medinan. From the school of Ibn 'Abbas is that the reciter of the prostration bows, and he cited as evidence His saying: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned penitently﴾ [Sad 38:24].

﴿Their sides forsake﴾: that is, they rise up and withdraw. It is said: "the man abandoned (jafa) the place": he left it. 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah said:
A Prophet whose side forsook his bed when the beds grew heavy with the polytheists.
Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: tajafi means withdrawing upward. "Al-madaji'" (beds) are the places of reclining for sleep, the singular being madja', meaning they are awake and do not know sleep. The majority (al-Jumhur) said: what is meant by this forsaking is voluntary prayer at night. This was the view of al-Awza'i, Malik, al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu al-'Aliyah and others. In a hadith, he mentioned the night prayer, then cited the verse as evidence, meaning the Messenger (ﷺ). Abu al-Darda', Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the forsaking of the side is to pray the 'Isha' and the Subh in congregation. Al-Hasan said: it is tahajjud; he also said, and 'Ata' said: it is al-'Atamah (the late night prayer). In al-Tirmidhi, from Anas: it was revealed concerning waiting for the prayer called al-'Atamah. Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: the voluntary prayers between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

﴿calling upon﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), or a resumed clause; ﴿in fear and hope﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), or two infinitives in the position of a circumstantial clause. The apparent meaning is that the du'a' is supplication (ibtihal) to God; it was also said: it is prayer (salah).

The majority recited ﴿what is hidden for them﴾ as a past passive verb (ukhfiya). Hamzah, al-A'mash and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the ya', as a present verb in the first person singular (ukhfi). Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-ma nukhfi" with the plural of majesty (nun). Al-A'mash also read "akhfaytu." Muhammad ibn Ka'b read "ma akhfa," as a past active verb. The majority recited ﴿from delight﴾ in the singular (qurrah). 'Abdullah, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, and 'Awf al-'Uqayli read "min qurrat," in the plural with alif and ta', and this is a transmission from Abu Ja'far and al-A'mash. The phrase ﴿ma ukhfiya﴾ may be a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or an interrogative (istifhamiyyah), in which case "ta'lam" is suspended (muta'allaqah). The clause is in the position of the object if "ta'lam" is transitive to one object; and in the position of two objects if it is transitive to two. Its explanation has already been given at ﴿the delight of the eyes﴾ [al-Qasas 28:9] in Ta-Ha. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Recite, if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of the delight of the eyes﴾." Ibn Mas'ud said: in the Torah it is written: "God has [prepared] for those whose sides forsake their beds what no eye has seen and no ear has heard," until the end.

﴿No soul knows﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it covers all souls, regarding what God, exalted is He, has stored for those people and concealed from all His creation, of what delights their eyes; no one knows it except Him. This is a great promise whose full reality and details the understandings cannot reach. Al-Hasan said: they concealed deeds in this world, so God concealed for them what no eye has seen and no ear has heard.

﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾: He, exalted is He, is the One who enables them to do righteous deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He thus cut off the hopes of those who wish." End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency.

﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a sinner?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: it was revealed concerning 'Ali and al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah. They quarrelled, and al-Walid said to him: "I am sharper of tongue than you, keener of spear, and more able to repel the troop." 'Ali said to him: "Be silent, for you are a sinner." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was revealed in general terms regarding believers and sinners, so it encompasses both and everyone in a similar situation." Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas said: it was revealed concerning 'Ali and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it. According to this, the verse is Meccan, because 'Uqbah was not in Medina; he was killed on the road to Mecca, returning from Badr. The plural in ﴿they are not equal﴾ and the division after it is taken according to the meaning of "man" (who). It was also said: ﴿they are not equal﴾ is in the dual, referring to the believer and the sinner, and the dual is a plural. Al-Zajjaj said: the revelation of the verse concerning 'Ali and al-Walid, then He explained the negation of equality by the position of each of them, in the singular. The majority recited ﴿gardens﴾ in the plural. It was said it was named this because, as is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: the souls of the martyrs take refuge in it. It was also said: it is on the right of the Throne. The majority recited ﴿nuzulan﴾ with a damma on the zay; Abu Haywah read it with a sukun. Nuzul is the provision of the one who descends (guest), then it became general for what is prepared for a guest.

﴿And as for those who sinned﴾: that is, by disbelief, ﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that what is meant is: 'so the garden of their refuge is the Fire,' that is, the Fire is for them in place of the garden of refuge for the believers, like His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾." End of quotation. This is far-fetched. One resorts to something like "so give them good tidings" only when it is explicitly stated, so that one says the punishment has taken the place of good tidings, just as "a painful blow" has taken the place of a greeting. As for supposing a hidden element for a speech that is self-sufficient and follows the best forms of eloquence, so that the speech is interpreted by supposing something, that is not good.

As for ﴿the lesser punishment﴾: Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: they are the calamities of this world in souls and property. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali said: it is killing by the sword, like the day of Badr. Mujahid said: killing and hunger for Quraysh; and it is reported from him: it is the punishment of the grave. Al-Nakha'i and Muqatil said: it is the years of drought in which God made them hungry. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the prescribed penalties (hudud). Ubayy also said: it is the strike, the constant punishment, and the smoke.

As for ﴿the greater punishment﴾: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: there is no disagreement that it is the punishment of the Hereafter. In al-Tahrir: most of them hold that the greater punishment is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection in the Fire. It was also said: it is killing, captivity and imprisonment. It is reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad that it is the emergence of the Mahdi with the sword. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾: Ibn Mas'ud said: perhaps whoever remains of them will repent. Abu al-'Aliyah said: perhaps they will repent. Muqatil said: they will return from disbelief to faith. It was also said: perhaps they intend to return and seek it, because of His saying: ﴿Return us, we will do righteousness﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:12]. The intention to return was called a return, just as the intention to stand was called standing in His saying: ﴿When you stand up for prayer, wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:6]. End of quotation. The opposite of "nearer" (al-adna) is "farther" (al-ab'ad), and of "greater" (al-akbar) is "smaller" (al-asghar). But the nearer includes the smaller, because it ends with the death of the one punished, and warning is suitable only with what is near, namely the immediate punishment. The greater includes the farther, because it occurs in the Hereafter, and warning with what is distant is suitable only by mentioning its magnitude and severity. Thus the contrast is achieved from the point of inclusion, and each of them comes out with what is more emphatic in warning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: from where is the interpretation of return as repentance correct? Perhaps 'la'alla' from God indicates intention, and when God intends something it happens and is not prevented; and their repentance is of what does not happen. Do you not see that if it were of what happens, they would not be tasting the greater punishment? I say: God's intention relates to His acts and the acts of His servants. When He intends one of His acts, it happens and is not prevented, because of His power and the sincerity of the purpose. As for the acts of His servants, either He intends them while they are free to choose them and necessitated to them by His compulsion and coercion; if He intends them and decrees them, then their ruling is the ruling of His acts. Or He intends them so that they choose them, while He knows they will not choose them; this does not detract from His power, just as your intention that your servant choose your obedience does not detract from your power, though he does not choose it, because his choice is not connected to your power, so after it, it does not indicate your incapacity." End of quotation. This is according to the Mu'tazilah's position, and the People of the Sunnah have refuted them, and that is established in the science of kalam (theology).

﴿from those who are reminded of the signs of their Lord, then turn away from them﴾: unlike the believers, who when reminded of them fall down prostrating.

﴿then turn away from them﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then" is for expressing remoteness. The meaning is that turning away from such signs of God in their clarity, their brightness, and their guidance to the right way, and attaining the supreme happiness after being reminded of them, is far-fetched in reason and custom, just as you say to your companion: "You found such an opportunity, then you did not seize it," expressing astonishment at his failure to seize it. From this is the "then" in the verse of the poet:
None removes the distress except a son of a free woman, who sees the agonies of death, then visits them.
End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 32, verses 13–22 (part 2 of 2):

He considered it unlikely that he would visit the throes of death after having seen them, been certain of them, and witnessed their severity. End of quote. (﴿مِنَ الْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾, "of the criminals") is general, covering everyone who commits crime (ijram), so that the greatest of wrongdoers is included in it by way of priority. Ijram here means: disbelief (kufr).

Yazid ibn Rufay' said: it refers to the people of qadar (divine decree and predestination debate), and he recited: ﴿إِنَّ الْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ up to his words: ﴿بِقَدَرٍ﴾ ("Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness. The Day they are dragged into the Fire on their faces, [it will be said], 'Taste the touch of Saqar. Indeed, We have created all things by due measure.'" [Qur'an 54:47–49]).

And in a hadith: "Whoever has three qualities has committed a crime: one who raises a banner in other than the right, one who disobeys his parents, and one who supports a wrongdoer." (ﷺ)

But the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together."﴾ ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this your Day. Indeed, We have forgotten you. A Prophet whose side forsook his bed when the beds grew heavy with the polytheists.

None removes the distress except a son of a free woman, who sees the agonies of death, then visits them.
End of quotation.

End of quotation.

And in a hadith: "Whoever has three qualities has committed a crime: one who raises a banner in other than the right, one who disobeys his parents, and one who supports a wrongdoer." (ﷺ)

The opposite of "nearer" (al-adna) is "farther" (al-ab'ad), and of "greater" (al-akbar) is "smaller" (al-asghar). Thus the contrast is achieved from the point of inclusion, and each of them comes out with what is more emphatic in warning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: from where is the interpretation of return as repentance correct? When He intends one of His acts, it happens and is not prevented, because of His power and the sincerity of the purpose. As for the acts of His servants, either He intends them while they are free to choose them and necessitated to them by His compulsion and coercion; if He intends them and decrees them, then their ruling is the ruling of His acts. It is reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad that it is the emergence of the Mahdi with the sword. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾: Ibn Mas'ud said: perhaps whoever remains of them will repent. Abu al-'Aliyah said: perhaps they will repent. Muqatil said: they will return from disbelief to faith. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: from where is the interpretation of return as repentance correct? When He intends one of His acts, it happens and is not prevented, because of His power and the sincerity of the purpose. As for the acts of His servants, either He intends them while they are free to choose them and necessitated to them by His compulsion and coercion; if He intends them and decrees them, then their ruling is the ruling of His acts. ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾: He, exalted is He, is the One who enables them to do righteous deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He thus cut off the hopes of those who wish." End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency.

﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a sinner?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: it was revealed concerning 'Ali and al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah. They quarrelled, and al-Walid said to him: "I am sharper of tongue than you, keener of spear, and more able to repel the troop." 'Ali said to him: "Be silent, for you are a sinner." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was revealed in general terms regarding believers and sinners, so it encompasses both and everyone in a similar situation." Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas said: it was revealed concerning 'Ali and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it. According to this, the verse is Meccan, because 'Uqbah was not in Medina; he was killed on the road to Mecca, returning from Badr. The plural in ﴿they are not equal﴾ and the division after it is taken according to the meaning of "man" (who). It was also said: ﴿they are not equal﴾ is in the dual, referring to the believer and the sinner, and the dual is a plural. Al-Zajjaj said: the revelation of the verse concerning 'Ali and al-Walid, then He explained the negation of equality by the position of each of them, in the singular. The majority recited ﴿gardens﴾ in the plural. It was said it was named this because, as is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: the souls of the martyrs take refuge in it. It was also said: it is on the right of the Throne. The majority recited ﴿nuzulan﴾ with a damma on the zay; Abu Haywah read it with a sukun. Nuzul is the provision of the one who descends (guest), then it became general for what is prepared for a guest.

﴿And as for those who sinned﴾: that is, by disbelief, ﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that what is meant is: 'so the garden of their refuge is the Fire,' that is, the Fire is for them in place of the garden of refuge for the believers, like His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾." End of quotation. This is far-fetched. One resorts to something like "so give them good tidings" only when it is explicitly stated, so that one says the punishment has taken the place of good tidings, just as "a painful blow" has taken the place of a greeting. As for supposing a hidden element for a speech that is self-sufficient and follows the best forms of eloquence, so that the speech is interpreted by supposing something, that is not good.

As for ﴿the lesser punishment﴾: Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: they are the calamities of this world in souls and property. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali said: it is killing by the sword, like the day of Badr. Mujahid said: killing and hunger for Quraysh; and it is reported from him: it is the punishment of the grave. Al-Nakha'i and Muqatil said: it is the years of drought in which God made them hungry. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the prescribed penalties (hudud). Ubayy also said: it is the strike, the constant punishment, and the smoke.

As for ﴿the greater punishment﴾: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: there is no disagreement that it is the punishment of the Hereafter. In al-Tahrir: most of them hold that the greater punishment is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection in the Fire. It was also said: it is killing, captivity and imprisonment. It is reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad that it is the emergence of the Mahdi with the sword. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾: Ibn Mas'ud said: perhaps whoever remains of them will repent. Abu al-'Aliyah said: perhaps they will repent. Muqatil said: they will return from disbelief to faith. It was also said: perhaps they intend to return and seek it, because of His saying: ﴿Return us, we will do righteousness﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:12]. The intention to return was called a return, just as the intention to stand was called standing in His saying: ﴿When you stand up for prayer, wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:6]. End of quotation. But the nearer includes the smaller, because it ends with the death of the one punished, and warning is suitable only with what is near, namely the immediate punishment. The greater includes the farther, because it occurs in the Hereafter, and warning with what is distant is suitable only by mentioning its magnitude and severity. Thus the contrast is achieved from the point of inclusion, and each of them comes out with what is more emphatic in warning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: from where is the interpretation of return as repentance correct? Perhaps 'la'alla' from God indicates intention, and when God intends something it happens and is not prevented; and their repentance is of what does not happen. Do you not see that if it were of what happens, they would not be tasting the greater punishment? I say: God's intention relates to His acts and the acts of His servants. When He intends one of His acts, it happens and is not prevented, because of His power and the sincerity of the purpose. As for the acts of His servants, either He intends them while they are free to choose them and necessitated to them by His compulsion and coercion; if He intends them and decrees them, then their ruling is the ruling of His acts. Or He intends them so that they choose them, while He knows they will not choose them; this does not detract from His power, just as your intention that your servant choose your obedience does not detract from your power, though he does not choose it, because his choice is not connected to your power, so after it, it does not indicate your incapacity." End of quotation. This is according to the Mu'tazilah's position, and the People of the Sunnah have refuted them, and that is established in the science of kalam (theology).

﴿from those who are reminded of the signs of their Lord, then turn away from them﴾: unlike the believers, who when reminded of them fall down prostrating.

﴿then turn away from them﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then" is for expressing remoteness. The meaning is that turning away from such signs of God in their clarity, their brightness, and their guidance to the right way, and attaining the supreme happiness after being reminded of them, is far-fetched in reason and custom, just as you say to your companion: "You found such an opportunity, then you did not seize it," expressing astonishment at his failure to seize it. From this is the "then" in the verse of the poet:
None removes the distress except a son of a free woman, who sees the agonies of death, then visits them.
End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 32, verses 13–22 (part 2 of 2):

He considered it unlikely that he would visit the throes of death after having seen them, been certain of them, and witnessed their severity. End of quote. (﴿مِنَ الْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾, "of the criminals") is general, covering everyone who commits crime (ijram), so that the greatest of wrongdoers is included in it by way of priority. Ijram here means: disbelief (kufr).

Yazid ibn Rufay' said: it refers to the people of qadar (divine decree and predestination debate), and he recited: ﴿إِنَّ الْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ up to his words: ﴿بِقَدَرٍ﴾ ("Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness. The Day they are dragged into the Fire on their faces, [it will be said], 'Taste the touch of Saqar. Indeed, We have created all things by due measure.'" [Qur'an 54:47–49]).

And in a hadith: "Whoever has three qualities has committed a crime: one who raises a banner in other than the right, one who disobeys his parents, and one who supports a wrongdoer." (ﷺ)

(p. 202) ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance. But the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together."﴾ ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this your Day. Indeed, We have forgotten you. Taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down prostrating and glorify the praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope, and they spend from what We have provided them.﴾ ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of the delight of the eyes, as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a sinner? They are not equal.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the Gardens of Refuge as a lodging, for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And as for those who sinned, their refuge is the Fire. ﴿We would have given every soul its guidance﴾: i.e., We would have created faith in it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "[This is] by way of compulsion and coercion. But We based the matter on choice, not on necessity, so they preferred blindness over guidance, and thus the word of punishment came into effect against the people of blindness rather than the people of sight. Do you not see what He follows it with, His saying: ﴿So taste [it] for your forgetting﴾? He made the tasting of the punishment a result of their action of forgetting the outcome and their scant reflection upon it, and their neglect of preparing for it. The meaning of forgetting is the opposite of remembering; that is, the indulgence in desires exhausted you and diverted you from remembering the outcome, and it dominated you so that you forgot it. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have forgotten you﴾ by way of correspondence, meaning: We have requited you with a recompense for your forgetting. The Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'ah) said: "It is permissible that He intends their guidance to the path of Paradise in the Hereafter, and He does not punish anyone; but the word from Him has come into effect that He will fill Hell, so it is not obligatory upon God to guide all of them to it. They said: rather, what is obligatory is the guidance of the infallible; as for one who has committed a sin, it is permissible for his guidance to be to the Fire as a recompense for his deeds. In the permissibility of that there is a prohibition, because they definitively hold that the intended meaning is guidance to faith." End of quotation.

﴿So taste﴾: the object of "taste" is omitted, or the object of "taste" is this punishment because of your forgetting ﴿the meeting of this your Day﴾, which is what you are in of humiliation of heads, disgrace and grief. The resumption with ﴿Indeed, We have forgotten you﴾ and the construction of the verb with inna and its noun indicates intensification of retribution against them.

This is contrary to the disbelievers' conduct of turning away from reminder, uttering abuse, and displaying arrogance. This prostration is one of the obligatory prostrations of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: prostration here means bowing (ruku'). It is reported from Ibn Jurayj: "the mosque is the place of bowing," meaning from this; and it follows from this that the verse is Medinan. From the school of Ibn 'Abbas is that the reciter of the prostration bows, and he cited as evidence His saying: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned penitently﴾ [Sad 38:24].

﴿Their sides forsake﴾: that is, they rise up and withdraw. It is said: "the man abandoned (jafa) the place": he left it. 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah said:
A Prophet whose side forsook his bed when the beds grew heavy with the polytheists.
Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: tajafi means withdrawing upward. "Al-madaji'" (beds) are the places of reclining for sleep, the singular being madja', meaning they are awake and do not know sleep. Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: the voluntary prayers between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

The apparent meaning is that the du'a' is supplication (ibtihal) to God; it was also said: it is prayer (salah).

The majority recited ﴿what is hidden for them﴾ as a past passive verb (ukhfiya). Hamzah, al-A'mash and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the ya', as a present verb in the first person singular (ukhfi). In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 32, verses 23–30:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, so do not be in doubt about meeting him. And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel.﴾ ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command, when they were patient and were certain of Our signs.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾ ﴿Has it not guided them how many generations We destroyed before them, among whose dwellings they walk? Indeed in that are signs. Will they not then listen?﴾ ﴿Have they not seen that We drive the water to the barren land and bring forth thereby crops from which eat their livestock and themselves? Will they not then see?﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this victory, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "On the day of victory, the disbelief of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be reprieved."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed they are waiting.﴾

When He had established the three principles, the prophethood, the beginning of creation and the return (to the Hereafter), He returned to the principle with which He had begun, which is the prophethood. It is not an innovation regarding prophethood, since messengers came before you. He mentioned Moses, peace be upon him, because of the nearness of his time (p. 205), and as an argument against those who follow his religion. He did not mention Jesus, because the majority of his law is derived from the Torah, and because the followers of Moses do not agree on his prophethood, whereas the followers of Jesus agree on the prophethood of Moses.

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah. Al-Hasan read "fi miryah" with a ḍammah on the mim. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to Moses, being a genitive attached to it in the sense of the object, and the subject is omitted, being the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ). That is: "from your meeting Moses," i.e. on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), meaning you witnessed him in reality, and he is the Prophet (ﷺ) who was given the Torah. The Messenger (ﷺ) described him, saying: "He is of medium height, with curly hair, as if he were one of the men of Shanu'ah when he saw him on the night of the Isra'." This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah and a group of the early generations (al-salaf). Al-Mubarrad said, when al-Zajjaj was tested with this issue. It was said that the pronoun refers to the Book; then it is either a genitive attached to it in the sense of the subject, with the object omitted, meaning "from the Book's meeting Moses and its reaching him," or the reverse, meaning "from Moses' meeting the Book and his receiving it." It was said that it refers to the Book with a hidden assumption, meaning "from the meeting of its like," i.e. We gave you the like of what We gave Moses, and We instructed you with the like of what was revealed to him, so do not be in doubt that you were instructed with its like and met its counterpart. Similar to this in meeting is His saying: ﴿And indeed you receive the Qur'an﴾ [al-Naml: 6]. Al-Hasan said: it refers to what the statement contains of the hardship and trial that Moses faced, because informing that He gave Moses the Book is as if He said: "And We certainly gave Moses this burden which you are on the path of, so do not doubt that you will be tested by people with what he was tested with." End of quote. This is a distant view. Even more distant is the one who made it refer to the Angel of Death mentioned earlier, the sentence being parenthetical. It was also said that it refers to the return to the Hereafter, and in the speech there is an inversion, the meaning being: "Then to your Lord you will be returned" [cf. al-Sajdah: 11].

﴿So do not be in doubt about meeting him﴾ means: about meeting (him in) the resurrection. These are reports that our book should have been free of recording, but the commentators have transmitted them, so we follow them. The pronoun in "wa ja'alnahu" (and We made it) refers to Moses, and this is the view of Qatadah. It was said that it refers to the Book, which He made a guide from misguidance. He singled out the Children of Israel for mention because they did not worship with what is in it, the descendants of Isma'il.

﴿And We made from among them﴾ means: from among the Children of Israel, ﴿leaders﴾ (a'immah), guides who are followed. The majority read "lamma sabaru" with a fatḥah on the lam and a shaddah on the mim. 'Abd Allah, Talhah, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ruways read it with a kasrah on the lam and a light mim. "Wa kanu" (and they were) may be coordinated with "sabaru," in which case it falls within the conditional clause. It may also be coordinated with "wa ja'alna minhum." 'Abd Allah also read "bima sabaru," with the preposition bi, and the pronoun in "minhum" apparently refers to the Children of Israel. "Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah. Al-Hasan read "fi miryah" with a ḍammah on the mim. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to Moses, being a genitive attached to it in the sense of the object, and the subject is omitted, being the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ). That is: "from your meeting Moses," i.e. on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), meaning you witnessed him in reality, and he is the Prophet (ﷺ) who was given the Torah. The Messenger (ﷺ) described him, saying: "He is of medium height, with curly hair, as if he were one of the men of Shanu'ah when he saw him on the night of the Isra'." This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah and a group of the early generations (al-salaf). Al-Mubarrad said, when al-Zajjaj was tested with this issue. It was said that the pronoun refers to the Book; then it is either a genitive attached to it in the sense of the subject, with the object omitted, meaning "from the Book's meeting Moses and its reaching him," or the reverse, meaning "from Moses' meeting the Book and his receiving it." It was said that it refers to the Book with a hidden assumption, meaning "from the meeting of its like," i.e. We gave you the like of what We gave Moses, and We instructed you with the like of what was revealed to him, so do not be in doubt that you were instructed with its like and met its counterpart. Similar to this in meeting is His saying: ﴿And indeed you receive the Qur'an﴾ [al-Naml: 6]. Al-Hasan said: it refers to what the statement contains of the hardship and trial that Moses faced, because informing that He gave Moses the Book is as if He said: "And We certainly gave Moses this burden which you are on the path of, so do not doubt that you will be tested by people with what he was tested with." End of quote. This is a distant view. Even more distant is the one who made it refer to the Angel of Death mentioned earlier, the sentence being parenthetical. It was also said that it refers to the return to the Hereafter, and in the speech there is an inversion, the meaning being: "Then to your Lord you will be returned" [cf. al-Sajdah: 11].

﴿So do not be in doubt about meeting him﴾ means: about meeting (him in) the resurrection. These are reports that our book should have been free of recording, but the commentators have transmitted them, so we follow them. The pronoun in "wa ja'alnahu" (and We made it) refers to Moses, and this is the view of Qatadah. It was said that it refers to the Book, which He made a guide from misguidance. He singled out the Children of Israel for mention because they did not worship with what is in it, the descendants of Isma'il.

﴿And We made from among them﴾ means: from among the Children of Israel, ﴿leaders﴾ (a'immah), guides who are followed. The majority read "lamma sabaru" with a fatḥah on the lam and a shaddah on the mim. 'Abd Allah, Talhah, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ruways read it with a kasrah on the lam and a light mim. "Wa kanu" (and they were) may be coordinated with "sabaru," in which case it falls within the conditional clause. It may also be coordinated with "wa ja'alna minhum." 'Abd Allah also read "bima sabaru," with the preposition bi, and the pronoun in "minhum" apparently refers to the Children of Israel. The judgment on the Day of Resurrection encompasses all creation.

﴿Has it not guided them﴾: the discussion of a verse like this in grammar, recitation and interpretation has preceded in Ta-Ha, except that here it says "min qablihim" (before them) and "yasma'una" (they listen), whereas there it says "qablahum" (before them) and "li-ulil-nuha" (for people of understanding). "Yasma'un" and "al-nuha" are verse-endings (fawasil).

﴿Have they not seen that We drive the water﴾: the Exalted established the proof against the disbelievers through the past nations who disbelieved and were destroyed. Then He established it against them by showing His power and alerting them to the resurrection. The explanation of "al-juruz" (barren) has preceded in al-Kahf, and every barren land falls under this, so it is not restricted to a specific place. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the land of Abyan in Yemen, a land watered by torrents and not by rain. It is also read "al-juzr" with a sukun on the ra'.

﴿So We bring forth thereby﴾: i.e. with the water. He singled out crops for mention, although God brings forth through it many kinds of fruits, vegetables and herbs useful in medicine and other things, to honour crops, and because it is the greatest of what is sought from plants. He placed "zar'" (crops) in the position of "nabat" (plants). The livestock were mentioned first, because what grows is eaten by livestock first, before the children of Adam eat the grain. Do you not see that al-qasil, which is barley sown for fodder, is eaten by livestock before it ears; and al-birsim (clover) and al-fisfisah (alfalfa) and the like are rushed upon by livestock before the children of Adam eat the grain of the crop. Or because it is food for beasts, and a human may nourish himself with other things, animal or otherwise. Or he began with the lower and then ascended to the more noble, who are the children of Adam. Abu Haywah and Abu Bakr in one narration read "ya'kulu" with the yā' from below. The majority read "yubsirun" with the yā' of the third person; Ibn Mas'ud read it with the tā' of address. The verse-ending "afala yubsirun" (will they not then see) came because what preceded is seen, whereas in the verse before it is heard, so "afala yasma'un" (will they not then listen) fits.

Then the Exalted informed about the disbelievers, that they hastened the decisive judgment between them and the Messenger (ﷺ), in the sense of mockery and denial. "Al-fath" (the victory) means the judgment, said by the majority, and this is what the statement "Say, 'On the day of victory'" etc. follows from. The view of al-Hasan and Mujahid that it is the conquest of Makkah is weak, because it does not correspond to what follows; for whoever believed on the day of the conquest of Makkah, his faith benefited him. Likewise the view of one who said it is the day of Badr. "Wa la hum yunzarun" means they will not be delayed from the punishment. When He knew their purpose in their question in the manner of mockery, and it was said to them: do not hasten it and do not mock, as though you have already arrived at that day and believed, and faith did not benefit you, and you asked for respite in the descent of punishment, but you were not respited. So "yawm" (day) is in the accusative, governed by "la yanfa'u" (will not benefit). Then He commanded him to turn away from them and await the victory over them and the triumph against them.

﴿Indeed they are waiting﴾ for the overcoming of you, in accordance with His saying: ﴿So wait; indeed we are waiting with you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52]. It was said: indeed they are waiting for the punishment, meaning this is their judgment, even if they do not perceive it. Al-Yamani read "muntaẓarun" with a fatḥah on the ẓā', as a passive participle; the majority read it with a kasrah, as an active participle, meaning "one who awaits their destruction," for they are deserving that their destruction be awaited. That is, they are certainly doomed; or: await that, for the angels in the heavens are waiting for it.
